title: Simple cells tuned to line orientation
asked: They asked how the activity of single cells relates to visual input.
did: They recorded simple cells in primary visual cortex (V1) while lines of different orientations moved through each cell’s receptive field.
found: Each cell responded to lines of particular orientations in a particular receptive field. One cell fired most strongly to upward movement of a line at about 315°.
means: A cell’s activity tells us what combination of features it represents. Psycholinguistics extends this idea of activation, as a metaphor, to word and concept representations.

title: Mediated priming in pronunciation but not lexical decision
asked: They asked whether activation spreads automatically beyond directly associated concepts in the memory network.
did: They built prime and target pairs, like lion and stripes, that were related only through a mediating concept, tiger. People either made a lexical decision about the target or read it aloud.
found: In lexical decision, directly related pairs like lion and tiger were faster, but mediated pairs were not faster than neutral or unrelated primes. In pronunciation, both directly related and mediated pairs were faster.
means: Activation does spread beyond directly related concepts. The mediated effect is small, and features of the lexical decision task masked it.

title: The case of Tan
asked: Broca asked what brain damage lay behind a patient who had lost the ability to speak.
did: He presented the case of “Tan” to the Society of Anthropology and later examined Tan’s brain.
found: Tan could produce only one jargon syllable but seemed to understand what was said. His brain had a large lesion that included the third convolution of the left frontal lobe, the inferior frontal gyrus.
means: This region became Broca’s area, and the case made relating specific functions to specific brain regions a respectable pursuit. Hughlings Jackson (1874) warned that locating the damage that destroys speech is not the same as locating speech.

title: Experimental lesions against phrenology
asked: Flourens asked whether specific parts of the cortex control specific senses, as phrenology implied.
did: He made experimental lesions, mainly in pigeons and rabbits, and observed what was lost.
found: He established distinct functions for the cerebral cortex, the cerebellum and midbrain structures. He found no match between specific cortical regions and specific senses, and when most of the cortex was removed, all senses were lost together.
means: Flourens argued that the size of a cortical lesion mattered more than its location, which opposed the idea of separate sense centers.

title: MRI of Broca’s original patients
asked: They asked exactly where and how far the damage extended in Broca’s landmark cases.
did: They scanned the preserved brains, including Leborgne’s, with MRI.
found: The lesion was very deep and included the insula, with heavy white matter damage to the superior longitudinal fasciculus. Other work by this group links speech apraxia to the insula rather than Broca’s area.
means: Broca’s anatomical localization was crude and probably wrong, because the speech problem he described may depend on deeper structures and connections.

title: PET subtraction for semantic processing of words
asked: They asked whether operations like recognizing word forms and computing word meaning can be localized in the brain.
did: They used PET with radio-labeled oxygen and subtracted control tasks from semantic tasks. Monitoring visual words for dangerous animals was compared with passive viewing, and generating uses was compared with repeating words, for visual and auditory input.
found: All three semantic contrasts activated the left inferior prefrontal cortex, a region corresponding roughly to Broca’s area.
means: Component operations on visual, phonological and semantic codes can be localized. Whole tasks like reading are not performed by any single brain area.

title: Simple recurrent networks that learn by prediction
asked: Elman asked whether a network that only learns to predict the next item can capture aspects of language.
did: He trained simple recurrent networks to predict the next letter in unspaced text, and the next word in simple sentences.
found: The letter network’s prediction error went down within words, so it found word boundaries in text like “manyyearsagoaboyandgirl.” The word network grouped words into grammatical classes and some semantic categories.
means: Word boundaries and word classes can emerge as side effects of prediction and gradual learning, without built-in rules.

title: A statistical model judges “colorless green ideas”
asked: Pereira asked whether a statistical model can tell Chomsky’s grammatical but novel sentence from its reversed version.
did: He trained a statistically based finite-state model, augmented with word categories, on newspaper text.
found: The model computed that “colorless green ideas sleep furiously” is 200,000 times more probable than “furiously sleep ideas green colorless.”
means: Statistics learned from experience can separate a grammatical novel sentence from an ungrammatical one, which challenges Chomsky’s claim that this judgment needs an internal grammar.

title: Priming resolves tip-of-the-tongue states
asked: The study asked whether hearing parts of a word helps people out of a tip-of-the-tongue state.
did: People were asked for a word from its definition, such as goods traded illegally for “contraband.” Those in a TOT state read a list with words sharing the first, middle or last syllable of the target, or none. Then they tried again.
found: People resolved their TOT states most often after words that shared the first syllable, like “contact.”
means: A TOT state is partial activation that falls short of the threshold for speaking. Shared sounds add activation to the missing word form and push it over the threshold.

title: Speech errors as linguistic evidence
asked: Fromkin asked whether the phoneme is a real unit of speech planning, or whether whole consonant clusters move as units.
did: She collected and classified spontaneous speech errors, including errors in words with consonant clusters.
found: Clusters get broken up all the time. “Fish grotto” became “frish gotto,” and “fresh clear water” became “flesh queer water.”
means: Single segments move independently of their clusters, so phonemes are units in speech planning. Her error data also supported a staged model of production.

title: Word frequency and picture naming time
asked: They asked how the frequency of an object’s name affects how quickly people name it.
did: People named pictures of objects. Later, the researchers matched high- and low-frequency names for length.
found: Naming time fell as frequency rose, in a log-linear relationship. After matching for length, there was still a robust frequency effect.
means: Frequent names are usually short, so the first result was confounded with length. The matched result means frequency effects are not merely length effects in disguise.

title: Matching word sets on many properties
asked: They needed word sets that differ on the property of interest while being equal on everything else.
did: They matched their word groups carefully on a wide range of lexical dimensions.
found: The matching was very thorough, but it left only ten words per cell, which is small for a word naming experiment.
means: Fine-grained matching removes confounds but can select odd items and create an artificial set of words.

title: Experiment 1, cyclic semantic blocking
asked: They asked why naming is slower for sets of semantically related pictures.
did: Participants named pictures over eight cycles in homogeneous blocks of related items, like duck, mouse, fish and snake. Other blocks were heterogeneous, with unrelated items like duck, saw, chair and bus. The same item appeared in both kinds of block in alternating cycles.
found: Naming got much faster after the first cycle, which is identity priming. Homogeneous blocks were slower than heterogeneous blocks, but only after all items had been named once.
means: Repetition helps while semantic context hurts. In WEAVER++, related lemmas compete, so selecting the target takes longer.

title: Visual similarity control
asked: They asked whether blocking might come from visual object recognition, because same-category objects can look alike.
did: They normed the stimuli so that same-category objects were not more visually similar on average. They also ran a control experiment that blocked visual similarity alone.
found: The visual control produced a different pattern, with an effect already in the first block.
means: The semantic blocking effect, which appears only after the first cycle, is not likely to come from visual similarity.

title: Simultaneous displays without a blocking effect
asked: The study looked for semantic blocking when people saw several objects at once.
found: They did not find a blocking effect.
means: This raised the possibility that blocking depends on seeing objects one at a time, which Belke, Meyer and Damian then tested.

title: Experiment 2, eye tracking during serial naming
asked: They asked whether blocking survives simultaneous displays, and which stage of production it affects.
did: Participants viewed four objects at once and named them in order while their eye movements were recorded. They measured gaze duration on each object, the lag from gaze leaving an object to its name starting, and speech duration.
found: Gaze duration showed a blocking effect after the first cycle. Lag showed no blocking effect, and speech duration got shorter with practice but showed no blocking.
means: Gaze duration is tied to lemma selection, so the semantic cost arises at lemma selection rather than phonological encoding or gestures.

title: Eye and mouth coordination in describing events
asked: Their demonstrations asked how looking is coordinated with speaking.
did: A speaker described the scene “The horse is kicking a cow” during a similar-object name block while eye movements were recorded.
found: The demonstration is labeled as accurately labeling a patient, the cow, during a similar-object name block.
means: Eye movements can be lined up with the words a speaker produces, so where and how long people look can be used to study production.

title: Experiment 3, blocking with new items
asked: They asked whether blocking generalizes to new items from the same categories.
did: New items from the same categories were introduced in cycle five.
found: Overall naming slowed down dramatically and the repetition priming effect went away, but the blocking effect remained.
means: Blocking is not a specific effect of repeating lists. It comes from the category being active, which fits competition at lemma selection.
